name: Workers’ Day: Mulweli’s Big Question
shortDescription: Mulweli thinks Workers’ Day simply means no school and no work—until Dad challenges him to discover the many people whose labour makes an ordinary day possible and the history behind the right to work, rest and live with dignity.
longDescription: Mulweli is delighted that 1 May means a day away from school, but Dad asks him a bigger question: who does the work that makes an ordinary day possible? Their conversation sends Mulweli on an imaginative journey through farms, mills, bakeries, clinics, taxis, streets and workplaces, where a loaf of bread becomes the first clue in a chain of shared labour. A magical twenty-four-hour clock introduces the idea that people need time for work, rest and life, leading into the history of the campaign for an eight-hour working day. Moving newspapers, posters and screen-printed historical scenes show the peaceful 1 May 1886 strike, the tragic Haymarket aftermath, the international growth of May Day and the role of organised workers in South Africa’s wider struggle for democratic rights. In the present day, Mulweli attends a welcoming Workers’ Day community gathering and notices that nurses, cleaners, drivers, food workers and other essential workers may still be on duty. When a gust damages the rally stage, workers use their different skills to repair it together, and Mulweli contributes by painting the work-rest-life clock onto the restored banner. By evening, he understands that Workers’ Day is about noticing work, remembering workers’ struggles and asking whether work is fair, safe and dignified. The Panda Kids Club adaptation uses a warm father-and-son story, rhythmic workplace teamwork and a hybrid illustrative CGI style in which history comes alive through moving posters, newspapers, clocks, drawings and workers’ artwork.

attribution.author: Eric Khorombi
attribution.adaptationNote: Adapted for animation by Panda Kids Club from the source title Workers’ Day and retitled Workers’ Day: Mulweli’s Big Question. The source story follows Mulweli asking his father why Workers’ Day is important. Dad explains the campaign for an eight-hour working day, the international origins of May Day, the role of worker organisation in South Africa and the continuing importance of fair pay and working conditions. The Panda Kids Club adaptation preserves this historical and civic foundation while restructuring the story into a sixteen-page active journey for Mulweli. Changes include giving Mulweli a challenge to identify the work behind an ordinary day; adding a breakfast-chain sequence linking farming, milling, baking, transport and trading; introducing a recurring twenty-four-hour WORK–REST–LIFE clock as the central visual teaching device; separating the peaceful 1 May 1886 strike from the 4 May Haymarket aftermath; representing the Haymarket tragedy symbolically rather than through graphic violence; expanding the international spread of May Day through a moving world-map and red-thread motif; showing South African workers organising across multiple occupations; highlighting the 1986 May Day stayaway as a major historical sequence; returning to the present day to show essential workers who continue working on public holidays; adding a community-rally problem in which workers use different skills to repair a damaged stage; and giving Mulweli an active role by painting the work-rest-life clock onto the repaired banner. The final page returns to the family living room, where Mulweli completes his assignment and understands Workers’ Day as a day to notice work, remember workers’ struggles and ask whether work is fair, safe and dignified. The visual adaptation uses premium hybrid illustrative CGI, hand-painted dimensional characters, moving poster and newspaper textures, screen-print historical sequences, rhythmic workplace staging and a contemporary South African colour palette.
